# What results did Hafele and Keating get flying atomic clocks around the world?

- On the eastward flight around the world, the flying atomic clocks lost 59 +/- 10 nanoseconds relative to the reference clocks at the U.S. Naval Observatory. (source: https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Relativ/airtim.html, 2026-11-08)
- On the westward flight around the world, the flying atomic clocks gained 273 +/- 7 nanoseconds compared to the naval observatory reference clocks. (source: https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Relativ/airtim.html, 2026-11-08)
- Relativity theory had predicted that the clocks would lose 40 +/- 23 nanoseconds going east and gain 275 +/- 21 nanoseconds going west. (source: https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Relativ/airtim.html, 2026-11-08)
- The recorded gains and losses agreed with relativistic predictions to within the expected experimental precision of approximately 10%. (source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafele%E2%80%93Keating_experiment, 2026-11-08)
- The empirical findings resolved the clock paradox using macroscopic timepieces. (source: https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Relativ/airtim.html, 2026-11-08)
- In October 1971, physicist Joseph C. Hafele and astronomer Richard E. Keating flew four cesium-beam atomic clocks around the world twice on commercial flights. (source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafele%E2%80%93Keating_experiment, 2026-11-08)
- The airborne clocks were compared against stationary ground clocks kept at the United States Naval Observatory. (source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafele%E2%80%93Keating_experiment, 2026-11-08)
- The experimental results were published in the journal Science, volume 177, on July 14, 1972. (source: https://www.dvidshub.net/news/printable/407785, 2026-11-08)
- Hafele and Keating published the report of their findings starting on page 166 of Science volume 177 in 1972. (source: https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Relativ/airtim.html, 2026-11-08)
